research.bottom_line:
The home router is end-of-life. Its last firmware is from 29 June 2020, and it has had no security fixes since. There is no Asuswrt-Merlin build for it, and no usable OpenWrt build: OpenWrt has no driver for the 5 GHz radio inside the BCM47189 chip.

(a) Isolation. Stock firmware has no setting for "this device may reach nothing on the LAN except AirPlay from the iPad". The guest network's "Access Intranet = Disable" option is all-or-nothing. It blocks the guest from the whole main LAN at layer 2, and that also blocks mDNS.
- Best free attempt: create one guest SSID on a single band (for example 5 GHz guest #1), set Access Intranet to Disable, and put both the projector and the iPad on it. Then test whether AirPlay works. Whether two guest clients can reach each other depends on the firmware version. On older pre-AiMesh firmware they could. Newer AiMesh-era firmware forces client isolation on the guest SSID (wlX.Y_ap_isolate=1).
- If they are isolated: the manual shows Telnet is available, and a known workaround is `nvram set wl1.1_ap_isolate=0`, then `nvram commit`, then reboot. Saving the guest settings in the web page undoes it.
- Side effect: with the projector on that guest SSID, the PC on the main LAN cannot reach ADB on port 5555. To install APKs over Wi-Fi, the PC would have to join the guest SSID for a while, which puts the PC next to the projector. Otherwise use the USB stick.

(b) Monitoring. Stock firmware can log every new outgoing connection: set Firewall > General > "Logged packets type" to Accepted or Both. It records source and destination IP and port only. You get no hostnames, no payloads, and no DNS queries sent to the router. Send the log to the PC with the "Remote log server" setting (UDP 514). Give the projector a fixed address with a DHCP Manual Assignment (up to 32 entries) so its lines are easy to filter. Traffic Monitor shows totals per interface only, not per device. This model has no AiProtection, no Traffic Analyzer and no Adaptive QoS. Per-device controls are limited to:
- Parental Controls time scheduling, with a per-MAC "Block" option that works as an internet kill switch
- the Network Services Filter (a blacklist by source IP and destination port)
- URL and keyword filters that apply to all devices

There is no DNS server setting per device. The DHCP DNS setting applies to every device. DNS-over-TLS needs ASUS firmware 386.4xxxx or later, so this router can never get it.

Cheapest add-ons, in order of preference:
1. A GL.iNet OpenWrt travel router plugged into a LAN port of the ASUS. The Opal GL-SFT1200 costs about €41 but has no AdGuard Home; the Beryl AX GL-MT3000 costs about $87–99 and has AdGuard Home. Put the projector and the iPad on its Wi-Fi so AirPlay works. Add one firewall rule dropping traffic from its LAN to 192.168.1.0/24. Optionally forward port 5555 from its WAN side to the projector, so the PC can reach the projector but not the other way round. This covers both (a) and (b), including DNS logs per device on models that support AdGuard Home.
2. Free, for probation only: Windows Mobile Hotspot plus the built-in pktmon, whose capture converts to pcapng for Wireshark. Downside: the projector sits next to the PC at 192.168.137.1. Run short sessions, keep the hotspot on the Public firewall profile, and keep file sharing off.
3. Pi-hole: DNS visibility only. It needs extra hardware or Docker, does not isolate anything, and hardcoded DNS or DNS-over-HTTPS in an app bypasses it.

Because the router itself is unpatched since 2020, also turn off UPnP, port forwarding and WAN web access, and plan to replace it eventually.

findings.claim: The home router is end-of-life. Its newest firmware is dated 29 June 2020, and no security updates will follow.
findings.detail: The ASUS support page lists the last firmware (2020/06/29) as the newest release. It fixed CVE-2020-12695 (CallStranger), an XSS, a directory traversal and CVE-2017-15653. The same page carries an EOL banner: firmware, utilities and the manual will no longer be updated. The ASUS EOL list includes the home router and names RT-BE50, RT-BE55, RT-BE58U V2 and ZenWiFi BD4/BD5 as replacements. Anything found after mid-2020 is unpatched on this router.

findings.claim: No Asuswrt-Merlin build exists, and OpenWrt is not practical: the router uses a BCM47189 (BCM53573 family) chip, and its 5 GHz 802.11ac radio has no Linux driver.
findings.detail: The Merlin site lists only RT-AX/BE models as supported, plus older RT-AC models as dropped, and the home router is in neither list. On openwrt-devel in November 2022, Arınç ÜNAL wrote that the 802.11ac PHY is in the BCM47189 SoC and has no support, and offered only a 2.4 GHz test image. On the OpenWrt forum, tmomas notes the G+/GP (BCM47189) and the GU (MT7621) are different devices, so RT-AC57U/GU images will not work. I found no newer source showing 5 GHz support.

findings.claim: The router has guest networks: up to 3 SSIDs per band (6 in total), each with an access time limit and an Access Intranet Enable/Disable setting.
findings.detail: From the router's manual (Spanish edition, pp. 26–27): guest SSIDs, authentication and encryption, an access time or 'Limitless', and 'Acceder a la intranet' Enable/Disable. ASUS's general FAQ says Access Intranet only works in wireless router mode. On firmware of this era, guest SSIDs share the main subnet; isolation is done with firewall/ebtables rules rather than a separate IP range.

findings.claim: Access Intranet = Disable blocks the guest from the whole main LAN at layer 2, including mDNS/Bonjour. There is no way to make an exception for one device in the web interface, so AirPlay between a guest device and a main-LAN device will not work.
findings.detail: eibgrad on SNBForums: guests share the private network, so there is no practical way to allow some devices and not others, and ASUS makes it all-or-nothing. On Merlin (RT-AC56U), medo64 had to add per-MAC ebtables FORWARD exceptions, plus ARP, to let a guest Chromecast talk to the main LAN, which shows the default drops all guest-to-LAN bridged frames. The UxPlay README says client/AP isolation on a guest network can block AirPlay discovery. I did not see the ebtables rules on this exact model; this is inferred from same-generation ASUSWRT.

findings.claim: Whether two clients on the same guest SSID can talk to each other depends on the firmware version. For the home router it has to be tested.
findings.detail: Old firmware (RT-AC68U on 378.55 and 380.64): with Access Intranet = No, guest clients could still reach each other. RMerlin said AP isolation was then a per-radio setting, not per guest network. Newer AiMesh-era web code, quoted by john9527, sets wl_ap_isolate=1 when guest LAN access is off, but only if amesh_support && amesh_wgn_support. On RT-AC86U, ColinTaylor and the original poster report guest clients isolated from each other, and enabling Access Intranet is the only way in the web page to lift that. I could not find whether the home router supports AiMesh; ASUS's AiMesh FAQ only points to product pages. Two guest SSIDs, such as wl0.1 and wl1.1, are separate interfaces, so the projector and the iPad must join the same guest SSID on the same band.

findings.claim: If guest clients turn out to be isolated, a command-line workaround can let them talk while keeping them off the main LAN: `nvram set wlX.Y_ap_isolate=0`, then `nvram commit`, then reboot. Saving guest settings in the web page reverts it.
findings.detail: eibgrad posted the commands for Merlin/RT-AC68U-era routers and warned that wireless config changes will likely undo it; two users confirmed it worked on Merlin. JWoo (RT-BE92U) also says saving guest settings resets the value to 1. The router's manual (p. 73) lists a Telnet enable option under Administration > System; SSH is not mentioned in that 2016 manual. Not verified on the last stock firmware for this model. This is the only stock-firmware route to 'projector + iPad on one segment, PC off it'.

findings.claim: Wireless > Professional has a 'Set AP Isolated' option, but it applies to a whole radio, not to one device or one SSID, so it cannot carve out the projector.
findings.detail: The manual (p. 50) says AP Isolated stops wireless clients from communicating with each other. RMerlin says the AP isolation option is only global, not per guest network. ASUS's own FAQ suggests it for blocking guests from wireless LAN devices, but it would also break AirPlay between the iPad and the projector.

findings.claim: The firewall can log every new outgoing connection ('Logged packets type' set to Dropped, Accepted or Both). This is the main monitoring tool on stock firmware.
findings.detail: Manual p. 68: Firewall > General has Enable Firewall, Enable DoS protection, and 'Logged packets type' (Dropped/Accepted/Both) for traffic between LAN and WAN. Merlin legacy firewall.c, which shares code with stock: when fw_log_x is accept or both, LAN forward rules use the 'logaccept' chain, which logs the first packet of each new connection with prefix 'ACCEPT ' before accepting it. Guest SSIDs are bridged into br0 on this firmware, so their traffic is logged too. Limits: IP and port only, no hostnames or payload, and DNS queries to the router are not logged. The log covers the whole household, so filter by the projector's fixed IP.

findings.claim: The system log can be sent to a remote syslog server (default UDP 514), such as the Windows PC, for logs that last through the probation period.
findings.detail: ASUS FAQ 1044954 describes the 'Remote log server' field (default port 514) and exporting syslog.txt. It does not give the exact menu on this model; a third-party guide places it under Administration > System. The router's 2016 manual's System page does not mention it, so it may only exist on newer 382 firmware; check in the web interface. The manual (p. 75) says the local log is cleared on reboot, while the FAQ (newer firmware) says it is kept, so assume it can be lost.

findings.claim: This model has no AiProtection, no Adaptive QoS and no Traffic Analyzer. Traffic Monitor shows totals per interface (WAN, wired, wireless), not per device.
findings.detail: The Blacktubi review of the home router says it has SmartQoS, with no Adaptive QoS and no AiProtection, plus parental control, guest network and a VPN client. The manual contents list 'Traffic Manager' with QoS and Traffic Monitor (p. 31: bandwidth for wired and wireless, daily view). ASUS's Traffic Monitor FAQ describes incoming and outgoing graphs for Internet, wired and wireless only. I found no per-device statistics page for this model.

findings.claim: Per-device controls available: Parental Controls time scheduling, a per-MAC 'Block' that works as an internet kill switch, and the Network Services Filter (blacklist or whitelist by source IP, destination port and schedule). The URL and keyword filters apply to everyone and are trivially bypassed.
findings.detail: The manual covers Parental Control (p. 32), Network Services Filter (pp. 70–71), URL filter and keyword filter (p. 69). The URL filter works through DNS; the keyword filter only matches page content, so neither sees much on HTTPS. ASUS FAQ: Time Scheduling picks clients by MAC and sets Disable, Time or Block per client. ASUS Network Services Filter FAQ: it blocks LAN-to-WAN packets; whitelist mode cuts internet for everyone not on the list during the schedule, so blacklist mode is the one usable for a single device. All of these filter only LAN-to-WAN traffic; none blocks LAN-to-LAN traffic. Android 11 MAC randomization could defeat MAC-based rules unless it is turned off for this SSID on the projector.

findings.claim: DHCP fixed-address leases exist (Manual Assignment, up to 32 MAC-to-IP entries). The DHCP DNS server setting applies to all devices, with no per-device DNS, and there is no DNS-over-TLS.
findings.detail: Manual p. 53: Enable Manual Assignment binds IPs to MACs, up to 32 entries, and there is one DNS server / WINS field. ASUS DHCP FAQ: the DNS field applies to all clients, and leaving it blank sends DNS to the router. ASUS DoT FAQ: DNS-over-TLS is only supported on firmware newer than 3.0.0.4.386.4xxxx, and this model stops at 382. For DNS per device, set a static IP and DNS on the projector itself (works only once the device is trustworthy) or use an add-on.

findings.claim: AirPlay (UxPlay, which the AirPlay Server app is built on) needs the iPad and the receiver on the same local network with mDNS on UDP 5353 working. Any isolation scheme must therefore keep the iPad on the projector's network segment.
findings.detail: UxPlay README: server and client must be on the same LAN; the service is announced via mDNS on UDP 5353; ports are random unless -p is used, which sets the legacy ports TCP 7100/7000/7001 and UDP 6000/6001/7011; guest-network client/AP isolation can block discovery. It also mentions a Bluetooth LE beacon alternative for networks without mDNS; I did not check whether the Android app supports it.

findings.claim: Recommended add-on: a GL.iNet OpenWrt travel router plugged into a LAN port of the ASUS, with the projector and the iPad on its Wi-Fi. One firewall rule (drop traffic from its LAN to 192.168.1.0/24) keeps both off the main LAN while internet still works.
findings.detail: On the OpenWrt forum, psherman recommends a rule that drops all traffic from the lan zone to 192.168.1.0/24; internet still works because the router itself reaches the upstream gateway. AirPlay works because the iPad and the projector share the GL network. For APK installs from the PC, a port forward of TCP 5555 from the GL's WAN side to the projector lets the PC reach the projector while the projector still cannot reach the PC; this follows from how NAT and that rule behave, and I have not tested it. Double NAT is normally fine for Netflix. AdGuard Home with DNS logs is supported on the GL-MT3000 Beryl AX, GL-A1300, GL-AXT1800 and others, but not on the GL-SFT1200 Opal or GL-MT300N-V2. To get logs per client, AdGuard Home must handle client DNS requests directly ('AdGuard Home Handle Client Requests'); with that option off, forum users report every query shows as localhost. Prices: Beryl AX about $86.90–98.99 (US store) or €101.99 (EU); Opal about €41 (EU). I did not verify that tcpdump installs on GL firmware.

findings.claim: Free option for the probation period only: Windows Mobile Hotspot plus the built-in pktmon gives a full packet capture viewable in Wireshark. The cost is that the projector sits directly next to the PC.
findings.detail: Microsoft Learn: pktmon is built into Windows from build 19041 and supports Wi-Fi capture and pcapng; 'pktmon etl2pcap <file> --out <name>' converts the capture for Wireshark. Hotspot clients get 192.168.137.x and the PC is 192.168.137.1. A tutorial says hotspot traffic falls under the Public firewall profile. Risk: any service listening on the PC (SMB, RPC, dev servers) is one hop from an untrusted device. Keep sessions short, keep the Public profile, turn off file sharing, and disconnect afterwards. This also does not test AirPlay unless the iPad joins the hotspot too; I did not verify whether hotspot clients can reach each other.

findings.claim: Pi-hole gives DNS visibility only: no isolation, extra hardware or Docker needed, and easy to bypass. AdGuard Home on a supported GL.iNet model does the same job and also isolates.
findings.detail: On this ASUS the DHCP DNS setting applies to all devices (manual p. 53), so a Pi-hole would cover the whole household unless DNS is set statically on the projector. An app with hardcoded DNS or DNS-over-HTTPS skips it. The GL.iNet AdGuard Home documentation covers the equivalent feature built into the router.

findings.claim: Hardening for the unpatched router: turn off UPnP, port forwarding and port triggering, so the projector cannot open inbound ports on its own, and keep web access from WAN disabled.
findings.detail: ASUS FAQ: WAN > Internet Connection > Enable UPnP = No, and it recommends turning off UPnP, Port Trigger and Port Forwarding together. Manual p. 73: web access from WAN is a toggle under Administration > System.

open_questions: On the last firmware, does setting a guest SSID to Access Intranet = Disable force client isolation (wlX.Y_ap_isolate=1)? Test: put the iPad and the projector on the same 5 GHz guest SSID and try AirPlay or a ping.
Does the home router support AiMesh? Not found on ASUS pages. It decides which guest-isolation code path applies.

Does the last stock firmware have SSH as well as Telnet, and does it have the Remote log server field? The 2016 manual shows Telnet only and does not mention remote syslog; check the Administration > System and System Log pages.
Can tcpdump be installed on GL.iNet stock firmware (Beryl AX / Opal), or does that need vanilla OpenWrt? Not verified.
Can clients of a Windows Mobile Hotspot reach each other? This matters only if AirPlay is to be tested while on the hotspot. Not verified.
Does the io.github.jqssun.airplay Android app support UxPlay's Bluetooth LE discovery beacon, which would allow AirPlay without mDNS on the same segment? Not checked.

checks.claim: The home router is end-of-life. Its last firmware is from 2020-06-29, and no security fixes will follow.
checks.note: The ASUS support page lists the last firmware (2020/06/29) as the newest build, with fixes for CallStranger, an XSS, a directory traversal and CVE-2017-15653. The page carries the EOL banner. The ASUS EOL list includes the home router and names RT-BE50, RT-BE55, RT-BE58U V2 and ZenWiFi BD4/BD5 as replacements. An NVD-derived CPE string 'home router firmware 3.0.0.4.386.46061' exists, but it comes from a vulnerability database entry for an RT-AC88U XSS bug, not from a real release. ASUS lists no 386 build for this model.

checks.claim: No Asuswrt-Merlin build exists, and OpenWrt is not practical: the 5 GHz 802.11ac radio inside the BCM47189 has no driver.
checks.note: The Merlin site does not list the home router, as supported or as dropped. Arınç ÜNAL (openwrt-devel, Nov 2022) says the 802.11ac PHY inside the BCM47189 has no support and offers only a 2.4 GHz test image. tmomas confirms the G+/GP (BCM47189) and the GU (MT7621) are different devices. OpenWrt's unsupported-features page marks BCM53xx WLAN as unsupported. Tenda AC9 owners, whose router uses the same SoC family, report no 5 GHz support either. I found nothing newer that adds 5 GHz.

checks.claim: Guest networks: up to 3 SSIDs per band (6 in total), each with an access time limit and Access Intranet Enable/Disable. Guests share the main subnet, and isolation is done with ebtables.
checks.note: Manual p.26 states 'hasta seis SSID (tres SSID de 2,4 GHz y tres SSID de 5 GHz)'. p.27 covers the access time limit (or unlimited) and the intranet on/off switch. The ASUS FAQ says Access Intranet only works in wireless router mode. Legacy ASUSWRT source (rc/lan.c, lanaccess_wl) walks lan_ifnames, the guest interfaces that sit in the LAN bridge, and applies ebtables rules. NGRhodes on SNBForums: 'AsusWRT does not use separate IP ranges for guests'.

checks.claim: Access Intranet = Disable blocks the guest from the whole main LAN at layer 2, mDNS included. The web interface has no way to make an exception for one device, so AirPlay between a guest device and a main-LAN device will not work.
checks.note: The research marked this as inferred, but the source code supports it. In legacy ASUSWRT rc/lan.c, lanaccess_mssid_ban() runs 'ebtables -A FORWARD -i <guest_if> -j DROP' and the matching '-o' rule, plus a broute rule for TCP to the LAN subnet. These drop every bridged frame between a guest SSID and the rest of br0, multicast mDNS and ARP included. They also block traffic between two different guest SSIDs, such as wl0.1 and wl1.1. medo64 had to add per-MAC ebtables exceptions plus ARP, which matches this. Caveat: the code is from the Merlin legacy tree, which shares code with stock 380/382. I could not inspect this model's own GPL build.

checks.claim: Whether two clients on the same guest SSID can reach each other depends on the firmware version, so it has to be tested on the home router.
checks.note: On 378.55 and 380.64, guests on the same SSID could see each other with Access Intranet off (MikeInNJ, Nasi Jose). john9527 quotes GUI code that forces wl_ap_isolate=1 when lanaccess is off, but only when amesh_support && amesh_wgn_support. RT-AC86U users report guests isolated from each other. I found no evidence either way on whether the home router supports AiMesh. ASUS's AiMesh FAQ and microsite only point to product pages, and the home router changelogs never mention AiMesh. The ebtables rules make the 'same SSID, same band' requirement follow directly.

checks.claim: If guests are isolated, `nvram set wlX.Y_ap_isolate=0`, then `nvram commit`, then reboot lets them talk while staying off the main LAN. Saving the guest settings in the web page reverts it.
checks.note: eibgrad's commands (RT-AC68U/Merlin) were confirmed by Bobcat00 and Mike S. JWoo (RT-BE92U Merlin, TUF-AX3000 V2 Gnuton) says saving the guest settings resets the value to 1, and eibgrad warns that wireless changes will likely undo it. ColinTaylor notes it only affects wireless-to-wireless traffic on the same AP. All the confirmations come from Merlin or Gnuton, none from stock 382 on this model. The manual (p.73) shows Telnet, so the commands should be possible. A non-persistent runtime variant, `wl -i wl1.1 ap_isolate 0`, is implied by odkrys's `wl -i wl0.1 ap_isolate 1` in thread 31447.

checks.claim: Wireless > Professional 'Set AP Isolated' applies to a whole radio, so it cannot carve out the projector. ASUS's own FAQ suggests it for blocking guests.
checks.note: Manual p.50 confirms it stops wireless clients from talking to each other. RMerlin: 'The AP isolation option is only available globally, not on a per-guest network basis', and Nasi Jose saw it affect the regular 2.4 GHz network. The second part is refuted: the current ASUS FAQ 1009857 (updated 2025-05-12) does not mention AP isolation at all.

checks.claim: Firewall 'Logged packets type' (Dropped/Accepted/Both) logs every new LAN-to-WAN connection with IP and port only, and guest traffic is included.
checks.note: Manual p.68 lists Dropped/Accepted/Both for LAN-WAN traffic. Legacy firewall.c: fw_log_x set to accept or both selects the 'logaccept' chain ('-A logaccept -m state --state NEW -j LOG --log-prefix "ACCEPT "'), and LAN-to-WAN forwarding uses '-A FORWARD -i br0 -j logaccept'. Guest interfaces are in the LAN bridge (see lan.c). Not checked: whether IPv6 forwarding is logged the same way. If the ISP provides IPv6, projector traffic over IPv6 could be missed.

checks.claim: The system log can be sent to a remote syslog server (UDP 514) such as the Windows PC.
checks.note: ASUS FAQ 1044954 describes the 'Remote log server' field with default port 514, but names no models. The router's manual pages 73 and 75 do not mention it, and p.75 says the log is cleared on reboot. A third-party guide places the field under Administration > System, and an RT-N56U user reported the field existing years earlier, so it probably exists on 382. Not confirmed for this model. Windows has no built-in syslog listener: the user would have to install a receiver and allow inbound UDP 514.

checks.claim: No AiProtection, no Adaptive QoS and no Traffic Analyzer. Traffic Monitor shows totals per interface, not per device.
checks.note: Blacktubi (Apr 2017): SmartQoS only, no Adaptive QoS and no AiProtection, both attributed to CPU limits. It also says AiCloud and Download Master are not available, which matters for the WrtHug risk. ASUS FAQ 114483: Traffic Monitor groups traffic as Internet, Wired and Wireless.

checks.claim: Per-device controls: Parental Controls time scheduling with a per-MAC 'Block' kill switch, plus the Network Services Filter (blacklist by source IP and destination port). URL and keyword filters apply to all devices.
checks.note: The Network Services Filter is confirmed: it filters LAN to WAN only, a blank source IP means every device, and whitelist mode cuts everyone else off. The URL and keyword filters are global (manual p.69). The per-client Disable/Time/Block modes appear only in the current ASUS FAQ, which is written for newer firmware. The router's manual (p.32) describes only per-MAC internet time limits, so the 'Block' mode is unverified on 382. A schedule that denies every time slot does the same job. On the URL filter mechanism, the manual says it relies on DNS, while the legacy code uses HTTP 'webstr' matching on TCP. Either way it is weak against HTTPS.

checks.claim: DHCP Manual Assignment allows up to 32 entries. The DNS server field applies to all clients, there is no per-device DNS, and there is no DNS-over-TLS.
checks.note: Manual p.53: up to 32 MAC addresses and a single DNS server field. The ASUS FAQ describes one DNS field for all DHCP clients, with a blank field meaning the router answers. The DoT FAQ: 'only supported on the firmware version later than 3.0.0.4.386.4xxxx', which this 382-only model will never get.

checks.claim: AirPlay through UxPlay and the AirPlay Server app needs the iPad and the receiver on the same LAN with mDNS (UDP 5353) working, so the iPad must share the projector's segment.
checks.note: UxPlay README: 'must be on the same local area network'. It names UDP 5353 for mDNS, and '-p' alone sets TCP 7100/7000/7001 and UDP 6000/6001/7011; ports are random otherwise. Its Windows troubleshooting section warns about client/AP isolation on guest networks. The jqssun android-airplay-server README says senders must be on the 'same subnet' and does not mention Bluetooth LE beacon discovery. UxPlay's beacon is a separate Python script that needs a Bluetooth adapter on the server side, so I found no BLE route for the Android app.

checks.claim: Add-on: a GL.iNet travel router on a LAN port of the ASUS, with the projector and the iPad on its Wi-Fi. A rule dropping traffic from its LAN to 192.168.1.0/24 isolates them, AdGuard Home provides per-client DNS logs, and the prices are Opal about €41 and Beryl AX about $87–99.
checks.note: psherman's rule is confirmed, described in words only. The thread does not cover DNS, but clients normally use the GL router as their resolver, so the rule does not affect them. The GL docs list GL-SFT1200 Opal and GL-MT300N-V2 among the models without AdGuard Home, and GL-MT3000 is not on that list. Correction: the cheapest AdGuard Home-capable model on the current store page is the Slate Plus GL-A1300 at $69.99, against $98.99 for the Beryl AX and $39.99 for the Opal. The store-eu and store-us URLs now redirect to gl-inet.com, so the € prices are unverified. The 'all clients show as localhost' thread is from GL firmware 3.x (MV1000, AR750S). The v4 docs say 'Handle Client Requests' makes AdGuard Home process client queries directly, but do not say it fixes per-client logs, so that is an inference. The port forward of TCP 5555 is untested, and it exposes ADB to every device on the main LAN, not only the PC. I found no confirmation that tcpdump installs on MT3000 firmware 4.x; a GL forum user needed an extra opkg feed on another model.

checks.claim: Free probation option: Windows Mobile Hotspot plus the built-in pktmon gives full captures for Wireshark. The hotspot uses 192.168.137.x and runs on the Public firewall profile.
checks.note: Microsoft Learn confirms pktmon is in-box on build 19041, supports Wi-Fi and can write pcapng ('pktmon etl2pcap <file> --out <name>'). The tutorial confirms the 192.168.137.x range with the PC at 192.168.137.1. It does not mention the firewall profile, so 'Public profile' is unverified. Wireshark itself has to be installed separately. I did not verify whether hotspot clients can reach each other, so AirPlay testing on the hotspot is unverified.

checks.claim: Pi-hole gives DNS visibility only, with no isolation, and it would cover the whole household because the ASUS DHCP DNS setting is global.
checks.note: Manual p.53 and the ASUS DHCP FAQ show a single DNS field for all clients. That an app with hardcoded DNS or DNS-over-HTTPS skips Pi-hole is general knowledge; I found no source specific to this device.

checks.claim: Hardening: turn off UPnP, port triggering and port forwarding, and keep web access from WAN disabled.
checks.note: ASUS FAQ 1045028 recommends turning off UPnP, Port Trigger and Port Forwarding together and gives the menu paths. Manual p.73 has the web-access-from-WAN toggle. Missing from the research: EOL ASUS routers are being actively hijacked. WrtHug (Nov 2025) uses AiCloud and lists the sibling model, but not the home router. AyySSHush (2025) enables SSH on port 53282 with an attacker key stored in NVRAM, which survives firmware updates. A factory reset and reconfiguration is the remedy.

verify.corrected_bottom_line:
The research mostly holds up. The facts that drive the plan are confirmed: the home router is EOL on its last firmware (2020-06-29), there is no Merlin build, and OpenWrt has no 5 GHz support. The guest-network mechanism is now confirmed in source code, not only inferred. With Access Intranet = Disable, legacy ASUSWRT (rc/lan.c) adds `ebtables FORWARD -i/-o <guest_if> -j DROP`. That cuts a guest SSID off from the main LAN and from the other guest SSIDs at layer 2, mDNS and ARP included, while internet, DHCP and DNS from the router keep working.

Stock-firmware plan (free):
- Put the projector and the iPad on the same single guest SSID (one band, for example 5 GHz guest #2) with Access Intranet off.
- Test AirPlay.
- If the two are isolated from each other, enable Telnet and run `nvram set wl1.2_ap_isolate=0; nvram commit; reboot` (or `wl -i wl1.2 ap_isolate 0` for a non-persistent test). Disable Telnet afterwards. Saving the guest page will likely undo it. This workaround is proven on Merlin and on other models, not on this one.
- Log the projector's outgoing connections with Firewall > Logged packets type = Accepted, filtered by its fixed DHCP address. This gives IPv4 IP and port only. IPv6 logging is unverified, so disable IPv6 during probation.
- Use a remote syslog server if the field exists on this firmware (likely, not confirmed). The PC needs a syslog receiver, which Windows does not include.
- Per-device kill switches: the Network Services Filter blacklist (confirmed), and parental-control scheduling per MAC. The newer 'Block' mode is unverified on 382; a deny-all schedule does the same job.
- No per-device DNS, no DoT, no AiProtection.

APK installs over Wi-Fi are possible with stock firmware. The PC cannot reach port 5555 across the guest boundary, so for each install session either:
- join the PC's Wi-Fi to the same guest SSID, or
- briefly turn Access Intranet on, then off again.

The USB stick or external drive stays as the fallback. ADB on the projector should require key authorization (RSA auth), not stay open.

Better paid option: a GL.iNet router on a LAN port of the ASUS, with the projector and the iPad on its Wi-Fi and a rule dropping LAN to 192.168.1.0/24 (check the real ASUS subnet first). AirPlay keeps working, the main LAN is isolated, and a TCP 5555 port forward gives one-way PC-to-projector ADB, though the forward is untested and open to the whole main LAN. Correction to the research's pick: the cheapest AdGuard Home-capable model on the current store page is the Slate Plus GL-A1300 ($69.99). The Beryl AX is $98.99, and the Opal at $39.99 has no AdGuard Home. Per-client DNS logs through 'Handle Client Requests' are inferred, not documented.

Before trusting the router's own logs, harden it:
- turn off UPnP, port forwarding, port triggering and WAN web access
- check Administration > System for unexpected SSH settings or keys (AyySSHush uses port 53282)
- factory-reset and reconfigure if anything looks wrong

Plan to replace the router; EOL ASUS models are being hijacked at scale (WrtHug, AyySSHush).

gaps.issue: The router itself is an untrusted EOL device: EOL ASUSWRT routers are being hijacked at scale. AyySSHush stores attacker SSH keys in NVRAM, which survives firmware updates; WrtHug names a sibling model. If the router is compromised, its own logs and isolation cannot be trusted. Check the SSH and authorized-key settings and look for port 53282; factory-reset and set a strong password before probation.

IPv6: the firewall logging and the Network Services Filter were checked only for IPv4. If the ISP provides IPv6, the projector could talk over IPv6 without showing up in the IPv4 logs. Disable IPv6 on the router during probation, or confirm that ip6tables logging works.

Not verified on this model's last firmware: whether a guest SSID with Access Intranet off forces client isolation (AiMesh support unknown), whether the nvram ap_isolate=0 workaround works and persists, whether SSH exists alongside Telnet, and whether the Remote log server field exists. All four need a check in the router's web interface or Telnet.

Remote syslog needs a third-party syslog receiver on Windows plus an inbound UDP 514 firewall rule; Windows does not include one. The router's local log is cleared on reboot (manual p.75) and fills quickly with household-wide 'Accepted' entries.
While the iPad is on the guest SSID it loses access to everything on the main LAN. The user has to switch the iPad's Wi-Fi when they want to cast, or keep it on the guest SSID permanently.

APK installs over Wi-Fi: every route found either puts the PC next to the projector (PC joins the guest SSID, or Access Intranet is briefly turned on) or exposes ADB to the whole main LAN (GL.iNet port forward). Nothing here covers securing the projector's ADB itself: turning off unauthenticated TCP 5555 and requiring RSA key approval, or Android 11 Wireless debugging with pairing. That belongs to the projector-hardening research but decides whether Wi-Fi installs are safe.

DNS hostnames: stock firmware cannot log the projector's DNS queries. The only per-client DNS log path found is AdGuard Home on a supported GL.iNet model. GL firmware 3.x showed every client as localhost; whether the v4 'Handle Client Requests' option fixes that is not documented.

I found no source for whether the AirPlay Server app runs on the projector's 32-bit armeabi-v7a userspace; its README names no supported ABIs. Its README also says DRM-protected content (for example the Apple TV app) is not supported, so some iPad apps will not cast.
Windows Mobile Hotspot: I could not confirm that hotspot clients can reach each other (needed to test AirPlay there) or that the hotspot network gets the Public firewall profile.

research.bottom_line: If the projector behaves like other H713 units, it runs Netflix at about 540p (Widevine L3, SD) through the sideloaded phone/tablet app, and the phone layout is awkward to use with a remote. Plan on that unless DRM Info shows otherwise. The Netflix Android TV app does not run on uncertified devices. Netflix says it only supports Android TV devices where it is listed in the Play Store, and the projector has no Play Store. Reviews of other H713 projectors from 2025 report Disney+ at about 720p and Prime Video at 480p. YouTube through SmartTube has no DRM, so it can reach the panel's full native resolution. SmartTube must come from its GitHub releases or F-Droid only: its signing key was compromised in December 2025, and builds from 30.55 on use a new key. microG is not worth adding. Widevine lives in the platform's DRM layer, not in Google Play Services, so microG cannot raise quality. Signature spoofing on stock Android 11 needs Zygisk + LSPosed hooks into system_server, which is new attack surface on a device you just cleaned. No source I found shows Netflix, Disney+ or Prime Video needing it. A Chromecast with Google TV, by contrast, is Netflix-certified Widevine L1: it plays 1080p (HD model) or 4K (4K model, capped by the panel's native resolution), with the proper TV app, remote and 5.1/Atmos. Recommendation: keep the paid DRM services (Netflix, Disney+, Prime) on the Chromecast. Use the projector's own Android for SmartTube, local files from the external drive, AirPlay and free or less-protected apps. One new risk: in at least one H713 firmware family, a Widevine L3 file bundle is put on the device by the malware, so after the cleanup check with DRM Info that Widevine still works.

findings.claim: H713 projectors ship with Widevine L3 only (no L1) and are not Google- or Netflix-certified, so paid streaming apps are capped at SD or near-SD.
findings.detail: Two separate reviews from 2025 of H713 / Android 11 units say the same thing. The androidpctv review of the Magcubic HY300 Pro (28 Apr 2025) lists 'DRM: Google Widevine L3', no audio/video certificates and no Google Play. The Simple Home Cinema review of the Magcubic L018 (15 Oct 2025, H713, Android 11 32-bit, 1 GB / 8 GB) says Netflix and Prime Video play 'at SD only'. A BadBox analysis of another H713 firmware (Sep 2026) also describes the device as uncertified and L3-only. Certification is granted per device and firmware, not per chip, so your own unit is still unverified. I found no H713 device with L1.

findings.claim: How to check the Widevine level: in the Netflix app go to App Settings > Playback Specification, which shows L1 or L3. The DRM Info app (com.androidfung.drminfo) also shows it.
findings.detail: Netflix's help page says HD on an Android phone or tablet needs Widevine L1, and that if Playback Specification shows L3 'you'll only be able to watch Netflix in SD'. ASUS documents the same menu path. DRM Info reads the MediaDrm API but is closed source, from a third-party developer. The Netflix menu avoids installing an extra APK. Running 'adb shell dumpsys media.drm' is a possible command-line check, but I could not confirm its output format on Android 11.

findings.claim: Netflix officially caps L3 Android devices at SD. The current phone/tablet app needs Android 9+, so Android 11 qualifies.
findings.detail: From the Netflix help page: the latest app needs 'Android OS 9 or later'; HD needs Widevine L1; with L3 'you'll only be able to watch Netflix in SD'. The same page warns that rooted or modified devices 'might not be able to download' the app, and that changes to certification status may stop it working properly. Netflix plans: Standard with ads and Standard are 1080p, Premium is 4K + HDR. On L3 the plan does not change the ceiling.

findings.claim: The Netflix Android TV app (com.netflix.ninja) does not work on uncertified Android TV devices.
findings.detail: Netflix's own article on error -13 says 'If you do not see the Netflix app in the Google Play Store, your device is not compatible with Netflix'. A Khadas forum thread (Aug 2023) shows the TV app failing with -13 on an uncertified box, and androidpctv says the Android TV app does not work on such boxes because of DRM protection. Workarounds exist but I don't recommend them. One is a modified ninja APK on GitHub (aidanmacgregor) that embeds a borrowed ESN, and its own ESN history shows Netflix blocking them after weeks or months. It is also untrusted modified code, which works against your security goal. The other, the Kodi Netflix add-on (CastagnaIT), says development is suspended and playback is SD at best 'when it works'. One more data point: the BadBox H713 firmware spoofs a Google ADT-3 identity and installs a ninja build. That suggests some vendors fake certification to get the TV app running.

findings.claim: The sideloaded phone/tablet Netflix app does run on H713 projectors without Google Play, at about 540p (SD) with stereo audio.
findings.detail: androidpctv's HY300 Pro review (Apr 2025, no Google Play, apps installed from APK) rates Netflix 'SD 540p, stereo'. Its older Netflix article (updated 2024) says recent phone versions reach 960x540. Simple Home Cinema (Oct 2025) also reports Netflix SD on an H713 unit. The old 2017 'rooted' block worked by hiding the Play Store listing; reports from then say sideloaded copies kept running.

findings.claim: The Netflix phone app does not appear to need Google Play Services or Play Integrity at runtime. Its certification gate is the Play Store listing.
findings.detail: The H713 review units have no Google Play and still play Netflix. GrapheneOS forum users report Netflix working without Google services when installed from outside the Play Store, and say Netflix's Play listing wrongly declares a SafetyNet/integrity requirement, which only hides the app in the store. Those posts are undated. On /e/OS (microG) results are mixed. I found no 2025-2026 source showing Netflix enforcing Play Integrity at runtime. Subscribing inside the app needs Google Play billing, so sign up on the web.

findings.claim: The 32-bit armeabi-v7a userspace is supported by Netflix phone 8.x builds up to at least Jan 2025. For the 2025-2026 9.x builds I could not confirm it.
findings.detail: APKMirror lists 8.x builds such as 8.96.1 and 8.114.0 as armeabi-v7a, Android 7.0+; the last 8.x is 8.143.1 (25 Jan 2025). Builds 9.30 (Aug 2025) and 9.50 (Jan 2026) exist, but their architecture did not show. I found no announcement of Netflix dropping 32-bit. The H713 reviews from 2025 do show Netflix running on 32-bit units.

findings.claim: Using the phone Netflix app on a projector needs a D-pad helper or an air mouse.
findings.detail: The BadBox H713 firmware ships com.android.nfx ('NFXAccessibility'), a Netflix D-pad navigation helper. The analyst judged it harmless: it is active only while com.netflix.mediaclient is in the foreground and has no INTERNET permission. androidpctv recommends a mouse or air mouse for the phone app. An HY320 buyer review also mentions a wireless mouse helping. Your Hotack firmware may have a similar helper; check before removing anything Netflix-related.

findings.claim: Risk after the cleanup: in one H713 firmware family the Widevine L3 file bundle is put on the device by the malware, so Widevine may need checking after cleaning or a reset.
findings.detail: The BadBox analysis (AT-M269 / HY300-clone firmware, build h713m_tuna_p3 Android 11) says plugin.jar 'drops a DRM key/licence bundle so streaming apps run on the uncertified device'. It goes into /data/mediadrm/IDM1013/L3/ and is downloaded as L3.zip from an RK3326 path. If your Hotack firmware relies on the same trick, wiping data or removing the dropper could leave Widevine unprovisioned, and DRM apps would then fail outright rather than drop to SD. Not verified for your HY320. Check DRM Info and the Netflix Playback Specification after cleanup, and keep /data/mediadrm in the eMMC backup.

findings.claim: Disney+ plays at about 720p on H713 L3 units. A sideloaded APK works on uncertified boxes, but whether it depends on Google services is mixed.
findings.detail: The HY300 Pro review rates Disney+ 'HD (720p)', and the L018 review says 'Disney+ caps at 720p'. androidpctv says Disney+ is hidden in Play on uncertified boxes and that manual APK install works. One GrapheneOS user had Disney+ stuck on its logo screen until Play was installed in a separate profile, while another ran it without Google Play Services. Whether current builds still include armeabi-v7a: not found.

findings.claim: Prime Video plays at SD (480p) on H713 L3 units, and Amazon's Appstore for non-Amazon Android devices closed on 20 Aug 2025.
findings.detail: The HY300 Pro review gives 'SD (480p)', and the L018 review says Prime Video plays at SD only. Since the Amazon Appstore shutdown, apps installed from it are 'not guaranteed to operate'. On the projector Prime Video would be another sideloaded APK. Google Play Services dependence: not found. The reviewed units ran it without Google Play.

findings.claim: YouTube: SmartTube needs no Google services and has armeabi-v7a builds. Get it only from its GitHub releases or F-Droid, because of the Dec 2025 signing-key compromise.
findings.detail: SmartTube's README says it does not require Google Services, needs Android 4.3+, and should not be downloaded from 'any app store, APK websites or blogs'. Official sources are GitHub releases, the kutt.to/stn_* links and F-Droid (app.smarttube.fdroid). Releases include armeabi-v7a APKs: stable 32.56 (23 Sep) and beta 32.68 (17 Oct). BleepingComputer (1-2 Dec 2025) reported the developer's signing keys stolen and a malicious libalphasdk.so in release builds (developer: 30.43-30.47; a 30.51 build was also found infected). The developer says 30.55 onward uses a new key; the BleepingComputer coverage says the fixed build installs as a separate app. Quality: YouTube is mostly DRM-free, so the decoder and panel set the limit. The reviews report HD on the 720p HY300 Pro and 1440p streams on the L018. The official Google YouTube TV app is a Google app that relies on Google services, which an uncertified device lacks.

findings.claim: RaiPlay: no evidence found on its Google Play Services or Widevine-level requirements on uncertified devices.
findings.detail: RaiPlay offers Rai account login and other non-Google logins, so a Google account doesn't seem required. Without signing in, only the live channels are available. The web version at raiplay.it is a fallback. Whether the Android or Android TV app runs without Google services, or what resolution it reaches on L3: not found. You'll have to test it.

findings.claim: microG is technically possible on rooted Android 11 but brings no streaming benefit and adds risk; skip it.
findings.detail: microG needs signature spoofing. On stock Android 11 that means Zygisk + LSPosed with FakeGApps: the microG wiki lists FakeGApps for Android 4.0-15 and the JingMatrix LSPosed fork for 8.1-16, and says ROM patchers 'still work properly only on Android < 9'. The 'microG Installer Revived' Magisk/KernelSU module promotes GmsCore to a privileged app but still needs separate spoofing. One 2021 report saw FakeGApps fail on Android 11 (NoSuchMethodError). Widevine is a vendor DRM HAL plugin in the platform ('Plugins are built by vendors or SOC makers and put in a /vendor partition'), so microG can't raise L3 to L1. A Sailfish thread notes microG has never provided Widevine. An uncertified, rooted device gets an empty Play Integrity device verdict ('genuine and certified Android device' is required for MEETS_DEVICE_INTEGRITY), so microG won't unlock apps that check integrity. Risks: code injected into system_server and every app, a spoofing permission any app can request, and more attack surface on a device whose firmware is already untrusted. Real GApps are no better: Google blocks sign-in on uncertified devices unless each Android ID is registered (2018 policy).

findings.claim: Netflix through the Chromecast into HDMI is far better: certified L1, 1080p or 4K, capped by the projector's native panel, with the TV interface, remote and surround audio.
findings.detail: Google says Chromecast with Google TV (HD) plays up to 1080p and the 4K model up to 4K, but only at a resolution the display supports. Netflix's Chromecast page lists 5.1 and Dolby Atmos support. Your Standard or Premium plan's 1080p would actually be delivered, against about 540p on the projector's own Android. The panel's native resolution (HY320 listings say 720p or 1080p) is the real ceiling. HDCP support on the H713 HDMI input is not documented anywhere I found, but if the Chromecast already plays Netflix on it, HDCP is fine. Which Chromecast model you have (Google TV HD/4K or an older cast-only one) is not known.

Does the Hotack HY320 firmware ship Google Play Services, a Netflix APK or a Netflix D-pad helper (like com.android.nfx)? List the packages before removing anything.
What is the panel's native resolution (listings say 720p or 1080p)? This sets the ceiling for both Chromecast and SmartTube.
Which Chromecast model do you have: Google TV HD, Google TV 4K, or an older cast-only one?
Do the current Netflix 9.x, Disney+ and Prime Video APKs still ship armeabi-v7a code? Not confirmed for 2025-2026 builds.
RaiPlay (and other Italian apps such as Mediaset Infinity): Google Play Services dependence and L3 resolution not found; they need testing on the device.

Searches for an L1 or Netflix-certified H713 device found nothing to refute the claim, only L1 projectors on other chips. Certification is per device, so the user's HY320 is still unverified.

APKMirror's listing confirms that DRM Info shows MediaDrm module info. Not verified: that DRM Info is closed source, and the ASUS FAQ (not opened). I found no example output for 'dumpsys media.drm', so it stays unconfirmed. The Netflix menu is enough and avoids an extra third-party APK.
